title: Gelatin Hydrolysis (Gelatinase) Test
principle: Some organisms produce extracellular proteolytic enzymes called gelatinases that hydrolyze gelatin, breaking down its protein structure so that a stab-inoculated gelatin medium remains liquid (fails to re-solidify on refrigeration) rather than setting back into a gel.
purpose: Used to differentiate organisms based on their ability to produce gelatinase, an accessory test in identification schemes for various Gram-positive and Gram-negative genera.
reagents: Nutrient gelatin medium (or equivalent gelatin-containing medium)

procedure.instruction: Stab-inoculate a tube of nutrient gelatin medium with the test organism using a straight inoculating needle.
Include an uninoculated gelatin tube as a negative/sterility control.
Incubate at the appropriate temperature for the organism for the manufacturer- or method-specified period.

Place the tube (and control) in a refrigerator for a short period before reading, since gelatin liquefied only by warm incubation temperature can re-solidify on cooling and must be distinguished from true enzymatic hydrolysis.
Observe whether the medium remains liquid after chilling.

positiveResult: Medium remains liquid (or only partially resolidifies) after chilling, indicating gelatinase activity.
negativeResult: Medium fully re-solidifies to a firm gel after chilling.
interpretation: A positive result indicates the organism secretes gelatinase capable of hydrolyzing the gelatin protein matrix; a negative result indicates it does not, under the conditions tested.
precautions: Always chill the tube before reading — gelatin naturally liquefies above roughly 25°C regardless of hydrolysis, so a warm tube can appear falsely positive.
Read alongside an uninoculated control tube to confirm the gelatin itself sets normally.
limitations: Gelatin hydrolysis can be slow; some protocols require observation over several days before calling a true negative.
Different gelatinases vary in activity by temperature and pH, so a single fixed incubation condition may not detect every gelatinase-producing strain equally well.
